claim: Gold particles were detected in the main body of the postsynaptic density as well as presynaptic mf terminals using immunogold labeling for GluN1.
source: Gold particles were detected in the main body of the postsynaptic density as well as presynaptic mf terminals (Figure 1A–C).
evidence: The claim is supported by electron microscopy data and immunogold labeling shown in Figure 1A-C.

claim: GluN1 localized in mf boutons in approximately 32% of presynaptic particles relative to the active zone.
source: GluN1 localized in mf boutons in a relatively high proportion to the active zone, as compared to associational–commissural (ac) synapse in the same CA3 pyramidal neuron (Figure 1D; mf, ~32% presynaptic particles; ac, <10% presynaptic particles; n = 3 animals).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of immunogold particle distribution shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Associational-commissural synapses in CA3 pyramidal neurons showed less than 10% presynaptic GluN1 particles.
source: GluN1 localized in mf boutons in a relatively high proportion to the active zone, as compared to associational–commissural (ac) synapse in the same CA3 pyramidal neuron (Figure 1D; mf, ~32% presynaptic particles; ac, <10% presynaptic particles; n = 3 animals).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of immunogold particle distribution shown in Figure 1D.

claim: AMPA receptors showed approximately 5% presynaptic localization in both mf and ac synapses.
source: Similar quantification for AMPA receptors did not reveal presynaptic localization of these receptors in either mf or ac synapses (Figure 1—figure supplement 1; ~5% presynaptic particles, n = 3 animals).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of AMPAR immunogold particle distribution shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Bath application of MK-801 (50 µM) significantly reduced low-frequency facilitation of AMPAR-EPSCs from 378 ± 57% to 270 ± 48%.
source: MK-801 significantly reduced LFF (baseline 378 ± 57%, MK-801 270 ± 48%, n = 10 cells, nine animals; baseline vs MK-801, p=3.8×10−5, paired t-test).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiological recordings and statistical analysis shown in Figure 1E.

claim: D-APV (100 µM) or R-CPP (50 µM) application reduced low-frequency facilitation from 546 ± 50% to 380 ± 38%.
source: D-APV (100 µM) or R-CPP (50 µM) application also reduced LFF (baseline 546 ± 50%, D-APV/R-CPP 380 ± 38%, n = 7 cells, five animals; baseline vs D-APV/R-CPP, p=0.00743, paired t-test).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiological recordings and statistical analysis shown in Figure 1F.

claim: Bath application of MK-801 (50 µM) significantly reduced low-frequency facilitation of KAR-EPSCs from 278 ± 40% to 195 ± 26%.
source: Bath application of MK-801 (50 µM) significantly reduced LFF (baseline 278 ± 40%, MK-801 195 ± 26% n = 8 cells, six animals; baseline vs MK-801, p=0.00259, paired t-test).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiological recordings of KAR-EPSCs with intracellular MK-801 shown in Figure 1G.

claim: Low-frequency facilitation of AMPAR-EPSCs remained stable in naïve slices (baseline 335 ± 62%, naïve 363 ± 63%).
source: In naïve slices (interleaved experiments), LFF remained unchanged throughout the recording session (baseline 335 ± 62%, naïve 363 ± 63%, n = 10 cells, nine animals; p=0.185, Wilcoxon signed-rank test, baseline vs naïve).
evidence: The claim is supported by control experiments shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Low-frequency facilitation of KAR-EPSCs was stable in naïve slices (baseline 274 ± 33%, naïve 278 ± 25%).
source: LFF of KAR-EPSCs was also stable in interleaved, naïve slices (baseline 274 ± 33%, naïve 278 ± 25%, n = 9 cells, six animals; p=0.236, Wilcoxon signed-rank test, baseline vs naïve).
evidence: The claim is supported by control experiments shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2B.

claim: CA3 pyramidal neurons patch-loaded with 2 mM MK-801 showed similar NMDAR-EPSC blockade by bath MK-801 as naïve cells.
source: Bath application of MK-801 (50 µM) blocked NMDAR currents in naïve cells to a similar magnitude as cells patch-loaded with MK-801 (n = 5 cells, four animals in each condition; U = 0.676, Mann–Whitney test).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: AAV5-CaMKII-Cre-GFP virus was bilaterally injected in the DG to selectively delete Grin1 in Grin1 floxed mice at postnatal days 16-20.
source: To this end, an AAV5-CaMKII-Cre-GFP virus was bilaterally injected in the DG to selectively delete Grin1 , whereas AAV5-CaMKII-eGFP was injected in littermates as a control at postnatal days 16–20 in both groups (Figure 2A).
evidence: The claim describes the experimental method used for genetic deletion of Grin1.

claim: No NMDAR-EPSCs were elicited in Grin1-cKO GCs voltage-clamped at +40 mV in the presence of 100 μM picrotoxin and 10 μM NBQX.
source: We confirmed that in contrast to control mice, no NMDAR-EPSCs were elicited by electrically stimulating medial perforant-path inputs in Grin1-cKO GCs voltage-clamped at +40 mV in the presence of 100 μM picrotoxin and 10 μM NBQX (Figure 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiological recordings confirming Grin1 deletion shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Grin1 deletion did not affect basal transmitter release as indicated by comparable paired-pulse ratios (Control: 2.5 ± 0.36, Grin1 cKO: 2.4 ± 0.31).
source: Grin1 deletion did not affect basal transmitter release as indicated by a comparable paired-pulse ratio to control (Control: 2.5 ± 0.36, n = 13 cells; Grin1 cKO: 2.4 ± 0.31, n = 13 cells; U > 0.5, Mann–Whitney test).
evidence: The claim is supported by paired-pulse ratio measurements and statistical analysis.

claim: Bath application of MK-801 (50 µM) significantly reduced low-frequency facilitation of KAR-EPSCs in transected mf axons from 213 ± 9% to 181 ± 10%.
source: Bath application of MK-801 (50 µM) significantly reduced LFF (baseline 213 ± 9%, MK-801 181 ± 10%, n = 8 cells, seven animals; baseline vs MK-801, p=0.002, paired t-test).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiological recordings in transected axons shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Low-frequency facilitation was stable in transected, naïve slices (baseline 186 ± 10%, naïve 196 ± 5%).
source: Stable LFF in transected, naïve slices (baseline 186 ± 10%, naïve 196 ± 5%, n = 8 cells, seven animals; baseline vs naïve, p=0.278, paired t-test).
evidence: The claim is supported by control experiments shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Puff application of D-APV (2 mM) in stratum lucidum significantly reduced low-frequency facilitation from 220 ± 19% to 176 ± 11%.
source: This manipulation significantly reduced facilitation (baseline 220 ± 19%, D-APV puff 176 ± 11%, n = 7 cells, seven animals; baseline vs D-APV puff, p=0.003, paired t-test).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiological recordings with local D-APV application shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Low-frequency facilitation remained stable during puff application of ACSF (baseline 210% ± 12, naïve 213% ± 9).
source: Stable LFF in acute slices during puff application of ACSF (baseline 210% ± 12, naïve 213% ± 9, n = 7 cells, seven animals; baseline vs naïve, p=0.778, paired t-test).
evidence: The claim is supported by control experiments shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Local D-APV puff application blocks NMDAR currents recorded at Vh = −50 mV and washes out in less than 10 min.
source: Local D-APV puff application (vertical arrow, two puffs at 0.1 Hz) blocks NMDAR currents recorded at Vh = −50 mV and washes out in less than 10 min (n = 7 cells, five animals, p=5×10−8, paired t-test).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: D-APV puff application in CA3 did not reduce NMDAR transmission in GCs.
source: D-APV puff application in CA3 did not reduce NMDAR transmission in GCs (n = 6 cells, five animals, control vs D-APV puff, U = 0.594, Mann–Whitney test).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Burst-induced facilitation measured as P5/P1 ratio was significantly reduced in Grin1-cKO animals (187 ± 16%) compared to control (255 ± 22%).
source: Burst-induced facilitation, triggered by light stimulation and measured as the ratio of EPSCs elicited by the fifth and first pulse (P5/P1 ratio), was significantly reduced in Grin1-cKO animals as compared to controls.
evidence: The claim is supported by optogenetic experiments shown in Figure 4C with statistical significance (p=0.0167).

claim: Bath application of MK-801 (50 µM) significantly reduced burst-induced facilitation of KAR-EPSCs from 601 ± 107% to 464 ± 84%.
source: bath application of MK-801 (50 µM) significantly reduced facilitation (baseline 601 ± 107%, MK-801 464 ± 84%, n = 13 cells, 10 animals; baseline vs MK-801, p=0.00042, paired t-test).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Burst-induced facilitation was stable in interleaved, naïve slices (baseline 369 ± 45%, naïve 367 ± 48%).
source: Burst-induced facilitation was stable in interleaved, naïve slices (baseline 369 ± 45%, naïve 367 ± 48%, n = 9 cells, nine animals; p=0.863, paired t-test).
evidence: The claim is supported by control experiments shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Bath application of MK-801 (50 µM) reduced KAR-mediated action potentials induced by burst-stimulation from 0.93 ± 0.17 to 0.46 ± 0.09 spikes per burst.
source: Bath application of MK-801 (50 µM) reduced KAR-mediated action potentials induced by burst-stimulation (baseline 0.93 ± 0.17, MK-801 0.46 ± 0.09, n = 6 cells, five animals; p=0.036, Wilcoxon signed-rank test).
evidence: The claim is supported by current-clamp recordings shown in Figure 4F.

claim: KAR-mediated action potentials were stable in interleaved naïve slices (baseline 0.76 ± 0.07, naïve 0.88 ± 0.1).
source: Stable KAR-mediated action potentials in interleaved naïve slices (baseline 0.76 ± 0.07, naïve 0.88 ± 0.1, n = 6 cells, five animals; p=0.2084, Wilcoxon signed-rank test).
evidence: The claim is supported by control experiments shown in Figure 4G.

claim: Bath application of MK-801 (50 µM) significantly reduced burst-induced facilitation of KAR-EPSCs from 450 ± 67% to 366 ± 63% under more physiological recording conditions.
source: Bath application of MK-801 (50 µM) significantly reduced burst-induced facilitation elicited by 5 pulses, 25 Hz (baseline 450 ± 67%, MK-801 366 ± 63%, n = 6 cells, four animals; baseline vs MK-801, p=0.036, Wilcoxon signed-rank test).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Burst-induced facilitation was stable in naïve slices under more physiological conditions (baseline 462 ± 63%, naïve 481 ± 71%).
source: Burst-induced facilitation was stable in interleaved, naïve slices (baseline 462 ± 63%, naïve 481 ± 71%, n = 5 cells, four animals; p=0.281, Wilcoxon signed-rank test).
evidence: The claim is supported by control experiments shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Bath application of MK-801 (50 µM) reduced AMPAR-mediated action potentials induced by burst stimulation from 2.47 ± 0.27 to 1.9 ± 0.24 spikes per burst.
source: Bath application of MK-801 (50 µM) reduced action potentials induced by 5 pulses at 25 Hz burst stimulation (baseline 2.47 ± 0.27, MK-801 1.9 ± 0.24, n = 6 cells, five animals; p=0.036, Wilcoxon signed-rank test).
evidence: The claim is supported by current-clamp recordings shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2A.

claim: AMPAR-mediated action potential firing was stable in naïve slices (baseline 1.55 ± 0.24, naïve 1.61 ± 0.23).
source: Stable action potential firing in interleaved naïve slices (baseline 1.55 ± 0.24, naïve 1.61 ± 0.23, n = 6 cells, five animals; p=0.402, Wilcoxon signed-rank test).
evidence: The claim is supported by control experiments shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Bath application of MK-801 (50 µM) blocked NMDAR currents of the fifth pulse to a similar magnitude as intracellular MK-801 during burst stimulation.
source: Bath application of MK-801 (50 µM) blocked NMDAR currents of the fifth pulse to a similar magnitude as iMK-801 (n = 5 cells, four animals per condition; U = 0.21, Mann–Whitney test).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claim: The NMDAR/AMPAR ratio was significantly reduced in Grin1-cKO GCs (0.13 ± 0.05) compared to control (0.90 ± 0.17) in calcium imaging experiments.
source: Summary plot (bottom) demonstrating that GluN1 deletion from GCs virtually abolished NMDAR-mediated transmission indicated by a strong reduction of NMDAR/AMPAR in Grin1-cKO granule cells as compared to controls (control 0.90 ± 0.17, n = 7 cells, six animals; Grin1-cKO 0.13 ± 0.05, n = 6 cells, six animals; control vs Grin1-cKO, p=3.81×10−7, unpaired t-test).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiological recordings confirming Grin1 deletion shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Calcium transients elicited by five action potentials at 25 Hz were significantly smaller in Grin1-cKO animals (0.025 ± 0.004 ΔG/R) compared to control (0.046 ± 0.01 ΔG/R).
source: We found that Ca2+ transients (CaTs) elicited by direct current injection in the GC soma (five action potentials, 25 Hz) were significantly smaller in Grin1-cKO animals as compared to control (Figure 5C–E).
evidence: The claim is supported by two-photon calcium imaging shown in Figure 5C-E with statistical significance (U = 0.017).

claim: D-APV (100 µM) significantly reduced the fifth peak of calcium transients from 0.155 ± 0.04 to 0.138 ± 0.03 ΔG/R.
source: D-APV (100 µM) significantly reduced the fifth peak (P5) of CaTs (baseline 0.155 ± 0.04, D-APV 0.138 ± 0.03, n = 13 boutons, three line scans per bouton, 10 animals; baseline vs D-APV, p=0.00642, Wilcoxon signed-rank test).
evidence: The claim is supported by two-photon calcium imaging under physiological Mg2+ concentration shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1D.

claim: The fifth peak of calcium transients is stable in naïve conditions (baseline 0.104 ± 0.026, naïve 0.105 ± 0.026).
source: In naïve conditions P5 of CaTs is stable (baseline 0.104 ± 0.026, naïve 0.105 ± 0.026, n = 12 boutons, three line scans per bouton, 10 animals; baseline vs naïve, p=0.255, Wilcoxon signed-rank test).
evidence: The claim is supported by control calcium imaging experiments shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1E.

claim: The first peak of calcium transients is not affected by D-APV (baseline 0.05 ± 0.017; D-APV 0.047 ± 0.014).
source: The first peak (P1) of CaTs is not affected by D-APV (baseline 0.05 ± 0.017; D-APV 0.047 ± 0.014; baseline vs D-APV, p=0.485, Wilcoxon signed-rank test) and is stable in naïve conditions (baseline 0.033 ± 0.009; naïve 0.032 ± 0.009, baseline vs naïve, p=0.196, Wilcoxon signed-rank test).
evidence: The claim is supported by calcium imaging analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Glutamate two-photon uncaging-induced calcium transients in dendritic spine heads of GCs were strongly reduced in Grin1-cKO animals (0.004 ± 0.003 ΔG/R) compared to controls (0.053 ± 0.01 ΔG/R).
source: We first confirmed that glutamate 2PU-induced CaTs in dendritic spine heads of GCs were strongly reduced in Grin1-cKO animals as compared to controls (Figure 6B,C).
evidence: The claim is supported by two-photon glutamate uncaging experiments shown in Figure 6B-C with statistical significance (p=0.00088).

claim: Grin1-cKO animals exhibited reduced ΔG/R signals compared to control regardless of laser power intensity.
source: To verify that reduced Ca2+ signals (ΔG/R) were a result of Grin1 deletion and not differences in uncaging laser power, we performed a laser power intensity–response curve and found that Grin1-cKO animals exhibited reduced ΔG/R signals as compared to control regardless of laser power intensity (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by laser power intensity-response curve analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Single glutamate uncaging pulses were insufficient to drive detectable calcium transients in control mf boutons.
source: We next measured glutamate 2PU-induced CaTs in mf giant boutons (identified as in Figure 5B) and found that single uncaging pulses were insufficient to drive detectable CaTs in control boutons (Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by two-photon glutamate uncaging experiments shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: A burst of two-photon glutamate uncaging stimulation (5 pulses, 25 Hz) induced calcium transients in mf boutons of control (0.014 ± 0.005 ΔG/R) but not in Grin1-cKO animals (−0.00012 ± −0.0006 ΔG/R).
source: However, a burst of 2PU stimulation (5 pulses, 25 Hz) induced CaTs in mf boutons of control but not in Grin1-cKO animals (Figure 6D,E).
evidence: The claim is supported by two-photon glutamate uncaging experiments shown in Figure 6D-E with statistical significance (p=0.015).

claim: Calcium transients elicited by two-photon glutamate uncaging were abolished by D-APV application.
source: Additionally, CaTs elicited by 2PU stimulation were abolished by D-APV application (Figure 6—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by two-photon glutamate uncaging experiments with D-APV shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 3.

claim: Control animals display robust ΔG/R signals compared to Grin1-cKO animals at varying laser power intensities.
source: Control animals display robust ΔG/R signals as compared to Grin1-cKO animals at varying laser power intensities (six spines, three line scans per spine, six animals per group, U = 0.00507 per power intensity, Mann–Whitney test).
evidence: The claim is supported by laser power intensity analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Repetitive pulses (5 pulses) result in larger ΔG/R signals compared to single pulses in mf boutons.
source: Repetitive pulses result in larger ΔG/R signals as compared to single pulses (n = 6 boutons, three line scans per bouton, six animals, p=0.03603, Wilcoxon signed-rank test).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of single vs. multiple pulse uncaging shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2C.

claim: D-APV application (100 µM) blocks calcium transients elicited by glutamate uncaging in mf boutons (baseline 0.0103 ± 0.0016, D-APV −0.004 ± 0.0024).
source: Summary data of D-APV block on glutamate uncaging elicited CaTs (baseline 0.0103 ± 0.0016, D-APV −0.004 ± 0.0024, n = 4 boutons, three line scans per bouton, three animals; U = 0.0304, Mann–Whitney test, baseline vs D-APV).
evidence: The claim is supported by two-photon glutamate uncaging experiments with D-APV shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 3C.

claim: GluN1-deficient mf boutons showed approximately 50% impairment in BDNF release compared to control during repetitive stimulation.
source: We found that GluN1-deficient mf boutons showed a significant (~50%) impairment in BDNF release as compared to control (Figure 7C–D).
evidence: The claim is supported by BDNF-pHluorin imaging experiments shown in Figure 7C-D.

claim: BDNF-pHluorin signal during the last 100 s reveals larger BDNF release in control animals (−18% ± 3%) compared to Grin1-cKO (−8 ± 1%) during repetitive stimulation.
source: Quantification of BDNF-pHluorin signal in (C) during the last 100 s reveals larger BDNF release in control animals as compared to Grin1-cKO (control −18% ± 3%, n = 9 slices, five animals; Grin1-cKO −8 ± 1%, n = 10 slices, five animals; Grin1-cKO vs control, p=0.00648, unpaired t-test).
evidence: The claim is supported by BDNF-pHluorin imaging analysis shown in Figure 7D.

claim: GluN1-lacking mf boutons displayed altered BDNF release compared to control during burst stimulation (5 pulses, 100 Hz, ×50).
source: Furthermore, using a more physiological pattern of burst stimulation, GluN1-lacking mf boutons still displayed altered BDNF release as compared to control (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by BDNF-pHluorin imaging with burst stimulation shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: BDNF-pHluorin signal during the last 100 s reveals larger BDNF release in control animals (−8.9% ± 2%) compared to Grin1-cKO (−3.5 ± 1%) during burst stimulation.
source: Quantification of BDNF-pHluorin signal in (B) during the last 100 s reveals larger BDNF release in control animals as compared to Grin1-cKO (control −8.9% ± 2%, n = 7 slices, five animals; Grin1-cKO −3.5 ± 1%, n = 11 slices, five animals; Grin1-cKO vs control, p=0.0305, unpaired t-test).
evidence: The claim is supported by BDNF-pHluorin imaging analysis shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Bath application of MK-801 (50 µM) had no significant effect on burst-induced depression or facilitation at mf-CA3 interneuron synapses.
source: We found that MK-801 bath application had no effect on burst-induced facilitation or depression (Figure 8B), suggesting preNMDARs do not play a role at mf-IN synapses in CA3.
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiological recordings from CA3 interneurons shown in Figure 8B.

claim: Bath application of MK-801 (50 µM) reduced low-frequency facilitation at mf-mossy cell synapses from 339 ± 41% to 258 ± 29%.
source: Similar to mf-CA3 synapses, we found that MK-801 reduced LFF (Figure 8C).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiological recordings from mossy cells shown in Figure 8C with statistical significance (p=0.00152).

claim: CA3 interneuron burst-induced facilitation of mf transmission was stable (baseline 273 ± 30%, naïve 294 ± 33%).
source: Stable CA3 IN burst-induced facilitation of mf-CA3 transmission (baseline 273 ± 30%, naïve 294 ± 33%, n = 10 cells, six animals; p=0.298, paired t-test, baseline vs naïve).
evidence: The claim is supported by control experiments shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Low-frequency facilitation of AMPAR-EPSCs in hilar mossy cells was stable (baseline 288 ± 51%, naïve 291 ± 29%).
source: Stable low-frequency facilitation (LFF) of AMPAR-EPSCs in hilar MCs (baseline 288 ± 51%, naïve 291 ± 29%, n = 7 cells, six animals; p=0.937, paired t-test, baseline vs naïve).
evidence: The claim is supported by control experiments shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Presynaptic NMDA receptors at mossy fiber boutons can be activated by physiologically relevant patterns of activity.
source: Here, we report that presynaptic NMDA receptors (preNMDARs) at mossy fiber boutons in the rodent hippocampus can be activated by physiologically relevant patterns of activity and selectively enhance short-term synaptic plasticity at mossy fiber inputs onto CA3 pyramidal cells and mossy cells, but not onto inhibitory interneurons.
evidence: The claim is stated in the abstract and supported by multiple experimental findings throughout the manuscript.

claim: Presynaptic NMDA receptors selectively enhance short-term synaptic plasticity at mossy fiber inputs onto CA3 pyramidal cells and mossy cells, but not onto inhibitory interneurons.
source: Here, we report that presynaptic NMDA receptors (preNMDARs) at mossy fiber boutons in the rodent hippocampus can be activated by physiologically relevant patterns of activity and selectively enhance short-term synaptic plasticity at mossy fiber inputs onto CA3 pyramidal cells and mossy cells, but not onto inhibitory interneurons.
evidence: The claim is stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data in Figures 1-4 and Figure 8.

claim: Presynaptic NMDA receptors facilitate brain-derived neurotrophic factor release at mossy fiber synapses.
source: Moreover, preNMDARs facilitate brain-derived neurotrophic factor release and contribute to presynaptic calcium rise.
evidence: The claim is stated in the abstract and supported by BDNF-pHluorin imaging data in Figure 7.

claim: Presynaptic NMDA receptors contribute to presynaptic calcium rise at mossy fiber boutons.
source: Moreover, preNMDARs facilitate brain-derived neurotrophic factor release and contribute to presynaptic calcium rise.
evidence: The claim is stated in the abstract and supported by two-photon calcium imaging data in Figures 5 and 6.

claim: Presynaptic NMDA receptors fine-tune mossy fiber neurotransmission by increasing presynaptic calcium.
source: Taken together, our results indicate that by increasing presynaptic calcium, preNMDARs fine-tune mossy fiber neurotransmission and can control information transfer during dentate granule cell burst activity that normally occur in vivo.
evidence: The claim is stated in the abstract and supported by calcium imaging and electrophysiology data throughout the manuscript.

claim: Presynaptic NMDA receptors can control information transfer during dentate granule cell burst activity that normally occur in vivo.
source: Taken together, our results indicate that by increasing presynaptic calcium, preNMDARs fine-tune mossy fiber neurotransmission and can control information transfer during dentate granule cell burst activity that normally occur in vivo.
evidence: The claim is stated in the abstract and supported by burst stimulation experiments in Figure 4.

claim: Anatomical evidence for presynaptic NMDA receptors arose from an immunoelectron microscopy study revealing NMDARs at the mossy fiber giant bouton of the monkey hippocampus.
source: Anatomical evidence for preNMDARs arose from an immunoelectron microscopy study revealing NMDARs at the mossy fiber giant bouton of the monkey hippocampus (Siegel et al., 1994), followed by functional studies in the entorhinal cortex, indicating that preNMDARs tonically increase spontaneous glutamate release and also facilitate evoked release in a frequency-dependent manner (Berretta and Jones, 1996; Woodhall et al., 2001).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous work (Siegel et al., 1994).

claim: Presynaptic NMDA receptors tonically increase spontaneous glutamate release in the entorhinal cortex.
source: Anatomical evidence for preNMDARs arose from an immunoelectron microscopy study revealing NMDARs at the mossy fiber giant bouton of the monkey hippocampus (Siegel et al., 1994), followed by functional studies in the entorhinal cortex, indicating that preNMDARs tonically increase spontaneous glutamate release and also facilitate evoked release in a frequency-dependent manner (Berretta and Jones, 1996; Woodhall et al., 2001).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work (Berretta and Jones, 1996; Woodhall et al., 2001).

claim: Presynaptic NMDA receptors facilitate evoked release in a frequency-dependent manner in the entorhinal cortex.
source: Anatomical evidence for preNMDARs arose from an immunoelectron microscopy study revealing NMDARs at the mossy fiber giant bouton of the monkey hippocampus (Siegel et al., 1994), followed by functional studies in the entorhinal cortex, indicating that preNMDARs tonically increase spontaneous glutamate release and also facilitate evoked release in a frequency-dependent manner (Berretta and Jones, 1996; Woodhall et al., 2001).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work (Berretta and Jones, 1996; Woodhall et al., 2001).

claim: The mossy fiber-CA3 synapse displays uniquely robust frequency facilitation both in vitro and in vivo.
source: This synapse displays uniquely robust frequency facilitation both in vitro (Nicoll and Schmitz, 2005; Salin et al., 1996; Vyleta et al., 2016) and in vivo (Hagena and Manahan-Vaughan, 2010; Vandael et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The molecular basis of short-term plasticity at mossy fiber synapses is not fully understood but likely relies on diverse presynaptic mechanisms that increase glutamate release.
source: The molecular basis of this short-term plasticity is not fully understood but likely relies on diverse presynaptic mechanisms that increase glutamate release (Jackman and Regehr, 2017; Rebola et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work (Jackman and Regehr, 2017; Rebola et al., 2017).

claim: Short-term, use-dependent facilitation is believed to play a critical role in information transfer, circuit dynamics, and short-term memory.
source: Short-term, use-dependent facilitation is believed to play a critical role in information transfer, circuit dynamics, and short-term memory (Abbott and Regehr, 2004; Jackman and Regehr, 2017; Klug et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work (Abbott and Regehr, 2004; Jackman and Regehr, 2017; Klug et al., 2012).

claim: The mf-CA3 synapse can strongly drive the CA3 network during short bursts of presynaptic activity.
source: The mf-CA3 synapse can strongly drive the CA3 network during short bursts of presynaptic activity (Chamberland et al., 2018; Henze et al., 2002; Vyleta et al., 2016; Zucca et al., 2017), an effect that likely results from two key properties of this synapse, namely, its strong frequency facilitation and proximal dendritic localization.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work (Chamberland et al., 2018; Henze et al., 2002; Vyleta et al., 2016; Zucca et al., 2017).

claim: Mossy fibers contain one of the highest expression levels of brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF).
source: Intriguingly, mfs contain one of the highest expression levels of brain-derived neurotrophic factor, BDNF (Conner et al., 1997).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous work (Conner et al., 1997).

claim: Presynaptic NMDA receptors were implicated in BDNF release at corticostriatal synapses.
source: While preNMDARs were implicated in BDNF release at corticostriatal synapses (Park et al., 2014), whether putative preNMDARs impact BDNF release at mf synapses remains unexplored.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous work (Park et al., 2014).

claim: Presynaptic NMDA receptors at mossy fibers may facilitate information transfer and provide an important point of regulation in the DG-CA3 circuit by modulating both glutamate and BDNF release.
source: Thus, preNMDARs at mfs may facilitate information transfer and provide an important point of regulation in the DG-CA3 circuit by modulating both glutamate and BDNF release.
evidence: The claim is stated in the Introduction and supported by experimental findings throughout the manuscript.

claim: Presynaptic NMDA receptors are adjacent to the release sites at mf-CA3 synapses.
source: In contrast, at mf-CA3 synapses, we found that preNMDARs are adjacent to the release sites, suggesting a direct control on glutamate release from mf boutons.
evidence: The claim is based on the electron microscopy data showing presynaptic localization of GluN1 near active zones.

claim: The reduction in facilitation of AMPAR transmission by NMDAR antagonism could be due to dampening of CA3 recurrent activity.
source: The reduction in facilitation of AMPAR transmission could be due to dampening of CA3 recurrent activity by NMDAR antagonism (Henze et al., 2000; Kwon and Castillo, 2008; Nicoll and Schmitz, 2005).
evidence: The claim is stated as a potential alternative explanation and is addressed by subsequent experiments.

claim: Presynaptic NMDA receptors facilitate neurotransmitter release in a target cell-specific manner.
source: We also found that preNMDARs facilitate neurotransmitter release in a target cell-specific manner.
evidence: The claim is stated in the Discussion and supported by data in Figure 8 showing differential effects on excitatory vs. inhibitory neurons.

claim: Presynaptic NMDA receptor facilitation of mf synapses onto glutamatergic neurons but not GABAergic interneurons may fine-tune the CA3 circuit by increasing the excitatory/inhibitory balance.
source: Thus, preNMDAR facilitation of mf synapses onto glutamatergic neurons but not GABAergic INs (Figure 8) may fine-tune the CA3 circuit by increasing the excitatory/inhibitory balance.
evidence: The claim is stated in the Discussion and supported by data in Figure 8.

claim: Presynaptic NMDA receptors may provide an important site of neuromodulatory control given the multiple signaling cascades known to regulate NMDARs.
source: Given the multiple signaling cascades known to regulate NMDARs (Lau and Zukin, 2007; Sanz-Clemente et al., 2013), preNMDARs at mf synapses may provide an important site of neuromodulatory control.
evidence: The claim is stated in the Discussion and supported by citations to previous work on NMDAR regulation.

claim: Presynaptic NMDA receptors could play a role in vivo during subtle presynaptic activities.
source: While most evidence, at least using robust induction protocols in vitro, indicates that long-term forms of presynaptic plasticity at mf synapses can occur in the absence of NMDAR activation (Castillo, 2012; Nicoll and Schmitz, 2005), our findings do not discard the possibility that preNMDARs could play a role in vivo during subtle presynaptic activities.
evidence: The claim is stated in the Discussion as a speculative possibility.

claim: Presynaptic NMDA receptors could regulate long-term synaptic plasticity by controlling BDNF release.
source: As previously reported for corticostriatal LTP (Park et al., 2014), preNMDARs could regulate long-term synaptic plasticity by controlling BDNF release, which is consistent with BDNF-TrkB signaling being implicated in mf-CA3 LTP (Schildt et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is stated in the Discussion and supported by citations to previous work.

claim: BDNF could facilitate glutamate release by enhancing NMDAR function at the presynapse.
source: In addition, BDNF could facilitate glutamate release by enhancing NMDAR function at the presynapse, as previously suggested (Chen et al., 2014; Madara and Levine, 2008), although the precise mechanism(s) remain unclear.
evidence: The claim is stated in the Discussion and supported by citations to previous work.

claim: By potentiating mf-CA3 transmission, BDNF could also promote epileptic activity.
source: By potentiating mf-CA3 transmission, BDNF could also promote epileptic activity (McNamara and Scharfman, 2012).
evidence: The claim is stated in the Discussion and supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Dysregulation of NMDARs is commonly implicated in the pathophysiology of brain disorders such as schizophrenia, autism, and epilepsy.
source: Lastly, dysregulation of NMDARs is commonly implicated in the pathophysiology of brain disorders such as schizophrenia, autism, and epilepsy (Lau and Zukin, 2007; Paoletti et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work (Lau and Zukin, 2007; Paoletti et al., 2013).

claim: Presynaptic NMDAR expression and function have been suggested to be altered in experimental models of disease, including neuropathic pain and epilepsy.
source: PreNMDAR expression and function have been suggested to be altered in experimental models of disease, including neuropathic pain (Chen et al., 2019; Zeng et al., 2006) and epilepsy (Yang et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work (Chen et al., 2019; Zeng et al., 2006; Yang et al., 2006).

claim: The development of specific presynaptic NMDAR tools is required to determine the functional impact of these receptors in vivo.
source: The development of specific preNMDAR tools is required to determine the functional impact of these receptors in vivo.
evidence: The claim is stated in the Discussion as a future direction.

claim: Dentate granule cells in vivo typically fire in brief bursts.
source: GCs in vivo typically fire in brief bursts (Diamantaki et al., 2016; GoodSmith et al., 2017; Henze et al., 2002; Pernía-Andrade and Jonas, 2014; Senzai and Buzsáki, 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work on in vivo GC firing patterns.

claim: Presynaptic NMDA receptors contribute to synaptic facilitation that occurs during physiologically relevant patterns of activity.
source: To test whether preNMDARs contribute to synaptic facilitation that occurs during more physiological patterns of activity, mfs were activated with brief bursts (five stimuli, 25 Hz).
evidence: The claim is supported by burst stimulation experiments in Figure 4.

claim: Presynaptic NMDA receptors, by facilitating glutamate release during bursting activity, could bring CA3 pyramidal neurons to threshold and trigger postsynaptic action potentials.
source: Lastly, we tested whether preNMDARs, by facilitating glutamate release during bursting activity, could bring CA3 pyramidal neurons to threshold and trigger postsynaptic action potentials.
evidence: The claim is supported by action potential recordings in Figure 4F-G.

claim: Presynaptic NMDA receptors at mf-CA3 synapses can contribute to information transfer from the DG to CA3.
source: Altogether, these results indicate that preNMDARs at mf-CA3 synapses can contribute to information transfer from the DG to CA3.
evidence: The claim is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 4.

claim: Presynaptic NMDA receptors could facilitate glutamate and BDNF release by increasing presynaptic Ca2+ rise.
source: PreNMDARs could facilitate glutamate and BDNF release by increasing presynaptic Ca2+ rise (Bouvier et al., 2016; Buchanan et al., 2012; Corlew et al., 2008; Park et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work and tested experimentally in Figures 5-7.

claim: Presynaptic NMDA receptors contribute significantly to presynaptic Ca2+ rise in mf boutons.
source: Thus, preNMDARs contribute significantly to presynaptic Ca2+ rise in mf boutons, and by this means likely facilitates synaptic transmission, although a potential contribution of Ca2+ rise-independent effects cannot be discarded.
evidence: The claim is stated in the Results section and supported by calcium imaging data in Figures 5 and 6.

claim: Brief bursts of glutamate two-photon uncaging, mimicking endogenous release during physiological patterns of activity, induces presynaptic Ca2+ influx in mf boutons by activating presynaptic NMDA receptors.
source: These findings indicate that brief bursts of glutamate 2PU, a manipulation that mimics endogenous release of glutamate during physiological patterns of activity, induces presynaptic Ca2+ influx in mf boutons by activating preNMDARs.
evidence: The claim is stated in the Results section and supported by two-photon glutamate uncaging data in Figure 6.

claim: Presynaptic NMDA receptors contribute significantly to BDNF release during repetitive or burst stimulation of mf synapses.
source: Taken together, our results suggest preNMDARs contribute significantly to BDNF release during repetitive or burst stimulation of mf synapses.
evidence: The claim is stated in the Results section and supported by BDNF-pHluorin imaging data in Figure 7.

claim: Presynaptic NMDA receptors enhance mf short-term plasticity in a target cell-specific manner.
source: Specifically, our results show that preNMDARs enhance mf short-term plasticity in a target cell-specific manner.
evidence: The claim is stated in the Discussion and supported by data in Figures 1-4 and Figure 8.

claim: By enhancing glutamate release onto excitatory neurons but not inhibitory interneurons, presynaptic NMDA receptors increase GC-CA3 spike transfer.
source: By enhancing glutamate release onto excitatory neurons but not inhibitory INs, preNMDARs increase GC-CA3 spike transfer.
evidence: The claim is stated in the Discussion and supported by data in Figures 4 and 8.

claim: Upon repetitive activity, presynaptic NMDA receptors promote BDNF release from mf boutons.
source: Lastly, upon repetitive activity, preNMDARs promote BDNF release from mf boutons.
evidence: The claim is stated in the Discussion and supported by BDNF-pHluorin imaging data in Figure 7.

claim: Presynaptic NMDA receptors act as autoreceptors to boost both glutamate and BDNF release at mf synapses.
source: Taken together, our findings indicate that preNMDARs act as autoreceptors to boost both glutamate and BDNF release at mf synapses.
evidence: The claim is stated in the Discussion and supported by experimental findings throughout the manuscript.

claim: By regulating information flow in the DG-CA3 circuit, presynaptic NMDA receptors may play a significant role in learning and memory.
source: By regulating information flow in the DG-CA3 circuit, preNMDARs may play a significant role in learning and memory.
evidence: The claim is stated in the Discussion as a speculative conclusion based on the experimental findings.

claim: Immunogold electron microscopy is a more precise localization method than immunoperoxidase electron microscopy.
source: Subsequent studies that used immunogold electron microscopy, a more precise localization method, identified NMDARs on the presynaptic membrane in a number of brain structures, including neocortex (Fujisawa and Aoki, 2003; Larsen et al., 2011), hippocampus (Berg et al., 2013; Jourdain et al., 2007; McGuinness et al., 2010), and amygdala (Pickel et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is stated in the Discussion and supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Presynaptic NMDA receptors are well positioned to modulate neurotransmitter release because they are close to the active zone.
source: Moreover, we found that these receptors are close to the active zone and therefore well positioned to modulate neurotransmitter release.
evidence: The claim is stated in the Discussion and supported by electron microscopy data in Figure 1.

claim: Somatodendritic potentials generated by NMDARs could signal to nerve terminals and lead to presynaptic Ca2+ elevations in the cerebellum and neocortex.
source: Previous work in the cerebellum and neocortex suggested that somatodendritic potentials generated by NMDARs could signal to nerve terminals and lead to presynaptic Ca2+ elevations (Christie and Jahr, 2008; Christie and Jahr, 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work (Christie and Jahr, 2008; Christie and Jahr, 2009).

claim: Changes in neurotransmitter release resulting from NMDAR antagonism could be due to somatodendritic NMDARs but not necessarily presynaptic NMDARs residing on nerve terminals.
source: Thus, changes in neurotransmitter release resulting from NMDAR antagonism could be due to somatodendritic NMDARs but not necessarily preNMDARs residing on nerve terminals (Duguid, 2013).
evidence: The claim is stated in the Discussion and supported by citation to previous work (Duguid, 2013).

claim: It is extremely unlikely that somatodendritic NMDARs could explain the reduction of short-term plasticity at mf synapses by NMDAR antagonism.
source: However, we showed that focal NMDAR antagonism far from the somatodendritic compartment and in transected axons still reduced short-term plasticity at mf synapses (Figure 3), making it extremely unlikely that somatodendritic NMDARs could explain our results.
evidence: The claim is stated in the Discussion and supported by experiments in Figure 3.

claim: Presynaptic NMDA receptors can operate as coincidence detectors at some synapses.
source: There is evidence that preNMDARs can operate as coincidence detectors at some synapses (Duguid, 2013; Wong et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work (Duguid, 2013; Wong et al., 2021).

claim: Presynaptic NMDA receptors contribute to low-frequency facilitation at the mf-CA3 synapse.
source: At the mf-CA3 synapse, we found that preNMDARs contribute to LFF (i.e. 1 s inter-stimulus interval).
evidence: The claim is stated in the Discussion and supported by data in Figures 1-3.

claim: Coincidence detection may not be an essential requirement for mf presynaptic NMDA receptors to modulate glutamate release.
source: However, coincidence detection may not be an essential requirement for mf preNMDARs to modulate glutamate release.
evidence: The claim is stated in the Discussion as an interpretation of the experimental findings.

claim: At resting membrane potential, the NMDAR conductance is not zero and the driving force for Ca2+ influx is high.
source: Of note, at resting membrane potential, the NMDAR conductance is not zero and the driving force for Ca2+ influx is high (Paoletti et al., 2013; Traynelis et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work (Paoletti et al., 2013; Traynelis et al., 2010).

claim: Mf presynaptic NMDA receptors may exhibit low-voltage dependence.
source: It is also conceivable that mf preNMDARs exhibit low-voltage dependence, as it has been reported at other synapses (Wong et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is stated in the Discussion as a speculative possibility supported by citation to previous work (Wong et al., 2021).

claim: The somatodendritic compartment of GCs can generate sub-threshold depolarizations at mf terminals (excitatory presynaptic potentials).
source: Remarkably, the somatodendritic compartment of GCs can generate sub-threshold depolarizations at mf terminals (a.k.a. excitatory presynaptic potentials) (Alle and Geiger, 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous work (Alle and Geiger, 2006).

claim: Excitatory presynaptic potentials might reduce the need for coincidence detection and transiently boost the functional impact of mf presynaptic NMDA receptors by alleviating the magnesium blockade.
source: By alleviating the magnesium blockade, these potentials might reduce the need for coincidence detection and transiently boost the functional impact of mf preNMDARs.
evidence: The claim is stated in the Discussion as a speculative mechanism.

claim: The presence of presynaptic NMDA receptors is downregulated during development in neocortex and hippocampus.
source: While the presence of preNMDARs is downregulated during development both in neocortex (Corlew et al., 2007; Larsen et al., 2011) and in hippocampus (Mameli et al., 2005), we were able to detect functional preNMDARs in young adult rats (P17–P28) and mice (P30–P44), once mf connections are fully developed (Amaral and Dent, 1981).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work (Corlew et al., 2007; Larsen et al., 2011; Mameli et al., 2005).

claim: Functional presynaptic NMDA receptors were detected in young adult rats (P17-P28) and mice (P30-P44), once mf connections are fully developed.
source: While the presence of preNMDARs is downregulated during development both in neocortex (Corlew et al., 2007; Larsen et al., 2011) and in hippocampus (Mameli et al., 2005), we were able to detect functional preNMDARs in young adult rats (P17–P28) and mice (P30–P44), once mf connections are fully developed (Amaral and Dent, 1981).
evidence: The claim is stated in the Discussion and supported by experimental data throughout the manuscript.

claim: Functional presynaptic NMDA receptors have been identified in axonal growth cones of hippocampal and neocortical neurons.
source: Functional preNMDARs have been identified in axonal growth cones of hippocampal and neocortical neurons, suggesting that these receptors are important for regulating early synapse formation (Gill et al., 2015; Wang et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work (Gill et al., 2015; Wang et al., 2011).

claim: Presynaptic NMDA receptors could play an important role at immature mf synapses and functional integration of new born GCs into the mature hippocampus.
source: Because GCs undergo adult neurogenesis, and adult-born GCs establish new connections in the mature brain, preNMDARs could also play an important role at immature mf synapses and functional integration of new born GCs into the mature hippocampus (Toni and Schinder, 2015).
evidence: The claim is stated in the Discussion as a speculative possibility supported by citation to previous work (Toni and Schinder, 2015).

claim: Experience can modulate the expression and composition of presynaptic NMDA receptors in neocortex.
source: Moreover, experience can modulate the expression and composition of preNMDARs in neocortex (Larsen et al., 2014), a possibility not investigated in our study.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous work (Larsen et al., 2014).

claim: The glutamate that activates presynaptic NMDA receptors may originate from the presynaptic terminal, the postsynaptic cell, nearby synapses or neighboring glial cells.
source: The glutamate that activates preNMDARs may originate from the presynaptic terminal, the postsynaptic cell, nearby synapses or neighboring glial cells.
evidence: The claim is stated in the Discussion as a general consideration.

claim: Activation of presynaptic NMDA receptors at mf synapses requires activity-dependent release of glutamate that likely arises from mf boutons.
source: Our results indicate that activation of preNMDARs at mf synapses requires activity-dependent release of glutamate that likely arises from mf boutons, although other sources cannot be discarded, including astrocytes.
evidence: The claim is stated in the Discussion and supported by experimental findings.

claim: At medial entorhinal inputs to GCs, presynaptic NMDA receptors appear to be localized away from the presynaptic release sites and facing astrocytes, consistent with preNMDAR activation by gliotransmitters.
source: For instance, at medial entorhinal inputs to GCs, preNMDARs appear to be localized away from the presynaptic release sites and facing astrocytes, consistent with preNMDAR activation by gliotransmitters (Jourdain et al., 2007; Savtchouk et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work (Jourdain et al., 2007; Savtchouk et al., 2019).

claim: The precise mechanism by which presynaptic NMDA receptors facilitate neurotransmitter release is poorly understood.
source: The precise mechanism by which preNMDARs facilitate neurotransmitter release is poorly understood, but it may include Ca2+ influx through the receptor and depolarization of the presynaptic terminal with subsequent activation of voltage-gated Ca2+ channels (Banerjee et al., 2016; Corlew et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is stated in the Discussion and supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The mechanism by which presynaptic NMDA receptors facilitate neurotransmitter release may include Ca2+ influx through the receptor and depolarization of the presynaptic terminal with subsequent activation of voltage-gated Ca2+ channels.
source: The precise mechanism by which preNMDARs facilitate neurotransmitter release is poorly understood, but it may include Ca2+ influx through the receptor and depolarization of the presynaptic terminal with subsequent activation of voltage-gated Ca2+ channels (Banerjee et al., 2016; Corlew et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work (Banerjee et al., 2016; Corlew et al., 2008).

claim: NMDA receptors have high Ca2+ permeability.
source: In support of this mechanism is the high Ca2+ permeability of NMDARs (Paoletti et al., 2013; Rogers and Dani, 1995).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work (Paoletti et al., 2013; Rogers and Dani, 1995).

claim: Presynaptic sub-threshold depolarization and subsequent activation of presynaptic voltage-gated Ca2+ channels is a common mechanism by which presynaptic ionotropic receptors facilitate neurotransmitter release.
source: Besides, presynaptic sub-threshold depolarization and subsequent activation of presynaptic voltage-gated Ca2+ channels is a common mechanism by which presynaptic ionotropic receptors facilitate neurotransmitter release (Engelman and MacDermott, 2004; Pinheiro and Mulle, 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work (Engelman and MacDermott, 2004; Pinheiro and Mulle, 2008).

claim: Presynaptic NMDA receptors may act in a metabotropic manner.
source: PreNMDARs may also act in a metabotropic manner (Dore et al., 2016) and facilitate spontaneous transmitter release independent of Ca2+ influx (Abrahamsson et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work (Dore et al., 2016; Abrahamsson et al., 2017).

claim: Presynaptic NMDA receptors may facilitate spontaneous transmitter release independent of Ca2+ influx.
source: PreNMDARs may also act in a metabotropic manner (Dore et al., 2016) and facilitate spontaneous transmitter release independent of Ca2+ influx (Abrahamsson et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous work (Abrahamsson et al., 2017).

claim: The open channel blocker MK-801 robustly reduced short-term plasticity at mf synapses, supporting an ionotropic mechanism that involves Ca2+ influx through presynaptic NMDA receptors.
source: Our findings demonstrating that the open channel blocker MK-801 robustly reduced short-term plasticity at mf synapses support an ionotropic mechanism that involves Ca2+ influx through preNMDARs.
evidence: The claim is stated in the Discussion and supported by experimental data in Figures 1-4.

claim: A previous study failed to observe Ca2+ reductions in mf boutons by DL-APV.
source: A previous study failed to observe Ca2+ reductions in mf boutons by DL-APV (Liang et al., 2002).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous work (Liang et al., 2002).

claim: A combination of factors could account for the discrepancy between the current study and a previous study that failed to observe Ca2+ reductions in mf boutons by DL-APV.
source: A combination of factors could account for this discrepancy with our study, including a stronger mf repetitive stimulation (20 pulses, 100 Hz), which may overcome a less potent NMDAR antagonism and/or the need for preNMDAR activity, as well as the use of a higher affinity Ca2+ indicator (Fura-2 AM) and a lower spatiotemporal resolution imaging approach.
evidence: The claim is stated in the Discussion as an explanation for discrepant findings.

claim: Presynaptic NMDAR activation by either repetitive activation of mfs or two-photon glutamate uncaging increases presynaptic Ca2+.
source: Nevertheless, in line with previous studies that detected presynaptic Ca2+ rises following local activation of NMDARs (e.g. NMDA or glutamate uncaging) in visual cortex (Buchanan et al., 2012) and cerebellum (Rossi et al., 2012), we provide direct evidence that preNMDAR activation by either repetitive activation of mfs or 2PU of glutamate increases presynaptic Ca2+ (Figures 5 and 6).
evidence: The claim is stated in the Discussion and supported by calcium imaging data in Figures 5 and 6.

claim: The Ca2+ targets of presynaptic NMDA receptors remain unidentified but may include proteins of the release machinery, calcium-dependent protein kinases and phosphatases, and Ca2+ release from internal stores.
source: Although the Ca2+ targets remain unidentified, these may include proteins of the release machinery, calcium-dependent protein kinases and phosphatases, and Ca2+ release from internal stores (Banerjee et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is stated in the Discussion and supported by citation to previous work (Banerjee et al., 2016).

claim: Presynaptic NMDA receptors can promote spontaneous neurotransmitter release as indicated by changes in miniature, action potential-independent activity.
source: In addition to facilitating evoked neurotransmitter release, preNMDARs can promote spontaneous neurotransmitter release as indicated by changes in miniature, action potential-independent activity (e.g. mEPSCs) (for recent reviews, see Banerjee et al., 2016; Kunz et al., 2013; Wong et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous reviews (Banerjee et al., 2016; Kunz et al., 2013; Wong et al., 2021).

claim: A potential role for presynaptic NMDA receptors in spontaneous, action potential-independent release at mf synapses cannot be discarded.
source: A potential role for preNMDARs in spontaneous, action potential-independent release at mf synapses cannot be discarded.
evidence: The claim is stated in the Discussion as a speculative possibility.

claim: Activation of presynaptic NMDA receptors by physiologically relevant patterns of presynaptic activity enhanced mf transmission and DG-CA3 information transfer.
source: Our results show that activation of preNMDARs by physiologically relevant patterns of presynaptic activity enhanced mf transmission and DG-CA3 information transfer (Figure 4).
evidence: The claim is stated in the Discussion and supported by data in Figure 4.

claim: NMDAR genetic deletion in GCs resulted in memory deficits (e.g. pattern separation).
source: A previous study reported that NMDAR genetic deletion in GCs resulted in memory deficits (e.g. pattern separation) (McHugh et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous work (McHugh et al., 2007).

claim: Memory deficits resulting from NMDAR genetic deletion in GCs could involve activity-dependent preNMDAR regulation of mf excitatory connections.
source: Although the mechanism is unclear, it could involve activity-dependent preNMDAR regulation of mf excitatory connections.
evidence: The claim is stated in the Discussion as a speculative mechanism.

claim: Presynaptic NMDA receptor specificity strongly suggests that these receptors have distinct roles in controlling information flow in cortical microcircuits.
source: Like in neocortex (Larsen and Sjöström, 2015), such specificity strongly suggests that preNMDARs have distinct roles in controlling information flow in cortical microcircuits.
evidence: The claim is stated in the Discussion and supported by citation to previous work (Larsen and Sjöström, 2015).

claim: Presynaptic NMDA receptors have been implicated in the induction of LTP and LTD at excitatory or inhibitory synapses in several brain areas.
source: PreNMDARs have been implicated in the induction of LTP and LTD at excitatory or inhibitory synapses in several brain areas (Banerjee et al., 2016; Wong et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous reviews (Banerjee et al., 2016; Wong et al., 2021).

claim: Long-term forms of presynaptic plasticity at mf synapses can occur in the absence of NMDAR activation using robust induction protocols in vitro.
source: While most evidence, at least using robust induction protocols in vitro, indicates that long-term forms of presynaptic plasticity at mf synapses can occur in the absence of NMDAR activation (Castillo, 2012; Nicoll and Schmitz, 2005), our findings do not discard the possibility that preNMDARs could play a role in vivo during subtle presynaptic activities.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work (Castillo, 2012; Nicoll and Schmitz, 2005).

claim: BDNF-TrkB signaling is implicated in mf-CA3 LTP.
source: As previously reported for corticostriatal LTP (Park et al., 2014), preNMDARs could regulate long-term synaptic plasticity by controlling BDNF release, which is consistent with BDNF-TrkB signaling being implicated in mf-CA3 LTP (Schildt et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous work (Schildt et al., 2013).

claim: In vivo evidence for the involvement of presynaptic NMDA receptors in brain function and disease is rather indirect.
source: At present, however, in vivo evidence for the involvement of preNMDARs in brain function and disease is rather indirect (Bouvier et al., 2015; Wong et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is stated in the Discussion and supported by citations to previous work (Bouvier et al., 2015; Wong et al., 2021).
